name: Sense Field
label: Revelation
lede: A Harbor City hardcore band grew into one of the first emo bands on Revelation, then lost five years to Warner Bros. and still got a hit out of the wreckage.

eras.title: Too many lineups to keep the name
eras.text: Jon Bunch and Chris Evenson spent the late '80s in Reason to Believe, a melodic hardcore band. Its sound kept moving and its members kept leaving, so in 1990 they stopped fighting it and started over as Sense Field.

years.h: Jon Bunch and Chris Evenson start Reason to Believe
years.p: Jon Bunch and Chris Evenson's first band, the melodic hardcore group Reason to Believe, makes two albums for Nemesis Records, The Next Door and When Reason Sleeps Demons Dance.

q: Reason to Believe was plagued with lineup changes.
years.h: Out of Reason to Believe, into Sense Field
years.p: In Harbor City, California, Jon Bunch and Chris Evenson regroup as Sense Field with guitarist [[Rodney Sellars|28e2e039-5b35-4aa4-ab62-4457cf077abd]], bassist John Stockberger and drummer [[Scott McPherson|c857aba4-942d-448c-b172-7807647c648d]]. The new name comes with a slower, more open sound.
years.xp:
Bunch said Reason to Believe simply couldn't hold a lineup together no matter how hard they tried. Sense Field was the reset.

Revelation's own bio credits Sense Field with pioneering the way for the emotional hardcore bands that followed.

eras.title: Jordan Cooper comes to a show
eras.text: Revelation co-founder Jordan Cooper saw Sense Field early and signed a Southern California band to a label still tied in most minds to New York straight edge. By Building in 1996 they were touring with Far, Texas Is the Reason and Jimmy Eat World, and Warner Bros. was listening.

years.h: Revelation signs Sense Field after Jordan Cooper sees them live
years.p: Revelation co-founder Jordan Cooper catches early Sense Field shows and brings the Harbor City band to the label.
Sense Field's self-titled album on Revelation, released at the height of grunge.
Another Sense Field release on Revelation the same year as the self-titled album. Jon Bunch remembered Killed for Less as the band's debut.

eras.title: Five years in limbo
eras.text: Signing with Warner Bros. was supposed to be the step up. Instead the label kept firing and rehiring people around Sense Field, their album Under the Radar sat unreleased, and the band waited out the rest of the '90s for somebody to put it out.

years.p: Sense Field's last Revelation album, licensed to Warner Bros. Warner signs the band the same year.

years.h: Live at Coney Island High, March 1996
yt: Live at Coney Island High, March 1996

eras.title: Save yourself
eras.text: Canadian independent Nettwerk picked Sense Field up, the shelved Under the Radar songs came back re-recorded, and Save Yourself gave the band its biggest moment more than a decade in. Then, in 2004, they stopped.

years.h: Tonight and Forever rescues the songs Warner shelved
years.p: Sense Field recorded Under the Radar for Warner Bros. in 1996, and the label never released it. Re-recorded, those songs became part of this 2001 Nettwerk album.
years.xp:
By Jon Bunch's account, Warner kept re-staffing, almost everyone who'd brought Sense Field in was fired, and the band had very few people left in its corner. Wikipedia puts the wait at five years.

Warner eventually let Sense Field out of the contract and allowed them to re-record the Under the Radar songs somewhere else.

years.cap: Sense Field play Save Yourself on network TV
years.p: Save Yourself lands on the Roswell soundtrack, gets Sense Field onto The Tonight Show and The Late Late Show, and puts Jon Bunch and Chris Evenson in Rolling Stone.
Sense Field's final album, and their only one to chart, reaching No. 37 on Billboard's Heatseekers.
Thirteen years after Reason to Believe became Sense Field, the band disbands.
After Sense Field ends, Jon Bunch sings on the Florida band's Hide Nothing and stays with Further Seems Forever until 2006.

eras.title: One more for Revelation, then a goodbye
eras.text: Revelation's 25th anniversary pulled bands back from all over its catalog, and Sense Field came too. Four years later the band played again without Jon Bunch, who had died, to raise money for his son.

years.h: Sense Field reunite for Revelation 25 in Pomona
years.p: Sense Field reunites for Revelation Records' 25th anniversary shows in Pomona, California.

years.h: Sense Field play Revelation 25 in Chicago
years.p: Sense Field play one more Revelation Records 25th anniversary show, in Chicago.

years.src: Broward Palm Beach New Times · Orange County Register via Wikipedia
years.h: Sense Field singer Jon Bunch dies at 45
years.p: Jon Bunch dies in Irvine, California; the Orange County coroner ruled it a suicide by overdose. He was singing in Lucky Scars, after stints in War Generation and Further Seems Forever.
years.xp: The Broward Palm Beach New Times, reporting the coroner's findings, said the autopsy showed high levels of diphenhydramine, the antihistamine in over-the-counter sleeping pills, along with small amounts of alcohol and methamphetamine, and heart disease from high blood pressure. Investigators found empty sleeping-pill packs in his car.

years.src: Billy Penn · Broward Palm Beach New Times
years.h: Sense Field play a benefit for Jon Bunch's son Jack
years.p: Sense Field reunite with guest singers at the TLA in Philadelphia, alongside [[Further Seems Forever|2bc3d11f-58fe-4adb-bfd9-6d316973005a]], [[Texas Is the Reason|b93c736f-a82f-4cae-9e57-a60b12d7055f]], [[Dag Nasty|4709dd69-1034-4634-9e88-d1099453b192]] and more, to raise a college fund for Jon Bunch's son. It follows a first benefit in Southern California.
years.xp:
Billy Penn reported fans and friends had already raised more than $65,000. Tour manager Jeremy Weiss insisted it was a rock concert, not a funeral.

On the bill: Garrett Klahn, Dave Smalley, Ari Katz and Into Another's [[Richie Birkenhead|7a1a6273-c31b-4828-8e20-0d6ea66943aa]].
